skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: find-skills
skills.description: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings. Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

result.content:
1. # View Design: `mm::phys::manager` (`PhysMemoryManager`)
2. 
3. > Phase output. Designs the abstract `View` that all later specs
4. > (`requires`/`ensures`) for the six in-scope functions will reference:
5. > `init`, `alloc_user_frame`, `check_user_watermark`,
6. > `alloc_many_user_frames`, `alloc_many_kernel_frames`, `alloc_kernel_frame`.
7. >
8. > Built **only** from `caller_analysis.md` and the body-removed public API
9. > (`body_removed_source.rs`), plus the **existing, do-not-modify** spec
10. > definitions (`byte_at_address`, `FrameAllocView`, `FrameAllocView::wf`,
11. > `Inner::inv`, `frame_addr_of`, `View for Inner`, `Inner::internal_inv`) and
12. > the already-committed subsystem View `PhysModView` / `phys_view()`.
13. 
14. ---
15. 
16. ## 1. Abstract Resource (from caller analysis)
17. 
18. To its callers (`mm/virt`, all through `unsafe { get_mut() }`), the
19. `PhysMemoryManager` is the **singleton broker over the global pool of physical
20. page frames**. It hands out *typed, owning frame handles*:
21. 
22. - **`KernelFrame`s** — drawn straight from the frame allocator, **contiguous on
23.   request**, **never watermark-gated** (kernel allocation must succeed whenever
24.   *any* physical frame is free).
25. - **`UserFrame`s** — drawn for user mappings and **watermark-gated**: a user
26.   request is rejected (`OutOfMemory`) if fulfilling it would drop the number of
27.   free frames below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`, so the kernel always keeps a reserve.
28. 
29. The only abstract state these six functions observe or mutate is therefore the
30. **frame partition**: which physical frames are allocated vs. free, with
31. per-frame refcounts, and — derived from it — *how many frames are free* (the
32. quantity the watermark gate reads). That partition is **already** modeled by the
33. do-not-modify `FrameAllocView` (== the verified `View for Inner` of the global
34. `frame::INSTANCE`, and == `PhysModView.frames`).
35. 
36. Callers explicitly **do not** observe: the `upool` internals, the
37. `MaybeUninit`/`AtomicBool` singleton storage, the watermark *threshold value*,
38. the chosen physical addresses, or how contiguity is obtained. They observe only:
39. *which frames became reserved*, *that user paths enforce the watermark*, *that
40. kernel bulk frames are contiguous*, and the *all-or-nothing / no-leak* error
41. behavior.
42. 
43. ---
44. 
45. ## 2. The View — reuse `FrameAllocView`, add no new struct
46. 
47. Because the six functions are `&mut self` methods, Verus already gives us the
48. `old(self)@ -> self@` transition pair for free — no global-token deferral is
49. needed for the *receiver* (unlike phys-mod's free functions). The receiver's
50. abstract state is exactly the frame partition it brokers, which is precisely
51. `FrameAllocView`. Wrapping it in a new one-field struct would add indirection
52. and zero information, so:
53. 
54. ```rust
55. impl View for PhysMemoryManager {
56.     type V = FrameAllocView;
57. 
58.     // Closed: the manager brokers the *global* frame partition (frame::INSTANCE).
59.     // The concrete mapping to that singleton is pinned in the proof phase by the
60.     // same ghost-token attachment PhysModView uses (see §8); here it is read like
61.     // any `self@`.
62.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> FrameAllocView;
63. }
64. ```
65. 
66. So `self@ : FrameAllocView`, and every spec for these functions speaks the
67. **existing frame-partition vocabulary** (`reserved`, `all_free`, `covers`,
68. `book_all`, the `allocated_frames`/`free_frames`/`refcounts` fields) plus the
69. small allocation/watermark extensions in §2.1.
70. 
71. ### 2.1 Derived spec helpers (new `impl FrameAllocView` block — existing `struct`/`wf` untouched)
72. 
73. ```rust
74. impl FrameAllocView {
75.     /// Number of frames currently free, i.e. available to hand out. This is the
76.     /// single quantity the kernel watermark reads. Models `frame::free_count()`.
77.     pub open spec fn free_count(self) -> nat {
78.         self.free_frames.len()
79.     }
80. 
81.     /// A user allocation of `count` frames is admissible: fulfilling it would
82.     /// still leave at least `KERNEL_WATERMARK` frames free for the kernel.
83.     /// This is the predicate behind the user-vs-kernel asymmetry — the gate
84.     /// `check_user_watermark` enforces. Reads the build-time constant directly
85.     /// so callers need not thread the threshold through.
86.     pub open spec fn user_alloc_ok(self, count: nat) -> bool {
87.         self.free_count() >= count + (config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK as nat)
88.     }
89. 
90.     /// Allocate a single currently-free frame `addr`: move it free -> allocated
91.     /// with refcount 1. (== `book_all(set![addr])`; spelled out for readability.)
92.     pub open spec fn alloc_one(self, addr: int) -> FrameAllocView {
93.         FrameAllocView {
94.             allocated_frames: self.allocated_frames.insert(addr),
95.             free_frames: self.free_frames.remove(addr),
96.             refcounts: self.refcounts.insert(addr, 1),
97.         }
98.     }
99. }
100. ```
101. 
102. The set-at-once transition already exists as the do-not-modify
103. `FrameAllocView::book_all(set)` — reused verbatim for the bulk paths.
104. Contiguity reuses the do-not-modify `region_frame_addrs(base, size)` (the set of
105. page-aligned frame addresses of `[base, base+size)`).
106. 
107. ---
108. 
109. ## 3. Well-formedness Invariant `inv()`
110. 
111. ```rust
112. impl PhysMemoryManager {
113.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
114.         // The brokered frame partition is well formed: free/allocated disjoint,
115.         // page-aligned, refcount<->allocated consistent, refcounts in 1..=255.
116.         self@.wf()
117.     }
118. }
119. ```
120. 
121. `inv()` is just `self@.wf()` and nothing more, on purpose:
122. 
123. - **Liveness is structural.** Possessing `&mut self` (only obtainable from
124.   `get_mut()` after `init` succeeded) already witnesses `manager_ready`; there is
125.   no separate "is-up" bit for these methods to carry. The cross-layer liveness
126.   fact lives in `PhysModView` (`manager_ready ==> initialized`) and is the
127.   business of `phys::init`, not of the per-allocation contracts.
128. - **The watermark is NOT an invariant.** "≥ `KERNEL_WATERMARK` frames free" holds
129.   only *after a user allocation*; kernel allocations are designed to dip below
130.   it. So it is a per-user-alloc **gate** (`user_alloc_ok`), never a type
131.   invariant. Putting it in `inv()` would be a false spec that kernel allocation
132.   legitimately violates.
133. 
134. ---
135. 
136. ## 4. Spec transitions of the target functions
137. 
138. State is `v = old(self)@`, `v' = self@` (both `FrameAllocView`). `ps` =
139. `spec_page_size()`, `W` = `KERNEL_WATERMARK`. Every clause is stated only over
140. `FrameAllocView`; nothing names `upool`, the singleton storage, or the threshold
141. value beyond `user_alloc_ok`.
142. 
143. > Frame-handle addresses: a `UserFrame`/`KernelFrame` exposes its physical frame
144. > address. Below this is written `f.addr()` — a thin spec accessor
145. > (`address()@` as `int`) to be added in the spec phase; the View commits only
146. > to *which address* each returned handle owns, not to the handle's storage.
147. 
148. ### 4.1 `alloc_kernel_frame(&mut self) -> Result<KernelFrame, Error>`
149. 
150. Kernel single frame; **no watermark**.
151. 
152. ```
153. requires  self.inv()
154. ensures   self.inv()
155.           match result {
156.             Ok(kf) => {
157.               // some previously-free frame is now reserved and owned by kf
158.               &&& v.free_frames.contains(kf.addr())
159.               &&& v' == v.alloc_one(kf.addr())
160.               // ⇒ v'.reserved(kf.addr())  and  v'.free_count() == v.free_count() - 1
161.             }
162.             Err(_) => {
163.               // nothing allocated, nothing leaked: partition unchanged
164.               &&& v' == v
165.               // failure ⇔ no frame was available at all (kernel never self-limits)
166.               &&& v.free_count() == 0
167.             }
168.           }
169. ```
170. 
171. `v.free_count() > 0 ==> result is Ok` is the contrapositive liveness fact a
172. caller relies on (kernel allocation succeeds whenever any frame is free).
173. 
174. ### 4.2 `alloc_user_frame(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error>`
175. 
176. User single frame; **watermark-gated**, identical gate to the bulk path at
177. `count == 1`. Fast path, no intermediate `Vec`.
178. 
179. ```
180. requires  self.inv()
181. ensures   self.inv()
182.           match result {
183.             Ok(uf) => {
184.               &&& v.free_frames.contains(uf.addr())
185.               &&& v' == v.alloc_one(uf.addr())
186.               &&& v.user_alloc_ok(1)              // the gate held before allocating
187.             }
188.             Err(_) => {
189.               &&& v' == v                          // unchanged, no leak
190.               &&& !v.user_alloc_ok(1)              // rejected ⇔ watermark would break
191.             }
192.           }
193. ```
194. 
195. Bidirectional gate: `result is Ok <==> v.user_alloc_ok(1)` (modulo pool
196. availability, which `user_alloc_ok` already implies via `free_count`). This is
197. exactly the CoW caller's mental model: `OutOfMemory` iff the watermark blocks it.
198. 
199. ### 4.3 `check_user_watermark(count: usize) -> Result<(), Error>` (private gate)
200. 
201. No external callers, no state change; it *is* the predicate `user_alloc_ok`.
202. 
203. ```
204. ensures   v' == v                                  // pure check, no mutation
205.           result is Ok  <==>  v.user_alloc_ok(count as nat)
206. ```
207. 
208. This single clause is what `alloc_user_frame` / `alloc_many_user_frames` reuse to
209. discharge their gate, so the two user paths provably enforce the watermark
210. *identically*.
211. 
212. ### 4.4 `alloc_many_user_frames(&mut self, count, frames: &mut Vec<UserFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
213. 
214. Bulk user; **watermark-gated**, **not** required contiguous. Caller supplies an
215. empty vector with capacity ≥ `count`.
216.

305. ## 5. Substitution test (per field / per helper)
306. 
307. > *"If the manager / frame allocator were rewritten with a different algorithm
308. > (buddy allocator, free-list, different singleton mechanism, different pool),
309. > would this still make sense?"*
310. 
311. | Element | Survives? | Reasoning |
312. |---------|-----------|-----------|
313. | `self@ : FrameAllocView` (the whole View) | ✅ | The allocated/free/refcount partition is what *any* physical-frame broker maintains; it is the existing `View for Inner`. A buddy/free-list rewrite still exposes the same `Set<int>` partition. Names no `upool`, bitmap, or refcount slice. |

320. `AtomicBool`, `Bitmap`, and `[u8; N]` refcount slice are *one* realization; the
321. View commits to none of them.

325. ## 6. Design rationale
326. 
327. - **Reuse the frame partition; introduce no new struct.** The six functions'
328.   sole caller-observable effect is on the global frame partition, which
329.   `FrameAllocView` already abstracts (and which `frame`'s verified `View for
330.   Inner` and `PhysModView.frames` already use). Setting `type V = FrameAllocView`
331.   keeps the manager specs interoperable with the `frame`-level contracts they
332.   call and honors the do-not-modify constraint. A wrapper struct would duplicate
333.   state and add indirection for no caller-visible gain.
334. - **`&mut self` gives the transition directly.** Unlike phys-mod's free
335.   functions, these are methods, so `old(self)@ -> self@` *is* the v->v' pair; no
336.   per-call global-token ceremony is needed in the contracts (only the closed
337.   `view()` mapping is pinned in proof — §8).
338. - **Watermark = a gate predicate, not an invariant.** `user_alloc_ok`
339.   (`free_count >= count + W`) is the one predicate distinguishing user from
340.   kernel allocation. It appears as a precondition-equivalent in the user paths
341.   and is deliberately absent from `inv()` because kernel allocation is *meant*
342.   to breach it. `check_user_watermark`'s contract is exactly this predicate, so
343.   both user paths provably share one gate.
344. - **Allocation expressed as set-booking.** `book_all(S)` (existing) /
345.   `alloc_one(addr)` describe the entire effect declaratively; `all_reserved`,
346.   `free_count` decrements, and "booked ⇒ never re-handed-out" all follow, so each
347.   ensures is a clause the caller drops straight into a proof.
348. - **Contiguity surfaced only where required.** Kernel bulk states
349.   `frames@[i].addr() == base + i*ps`; user bulk states only a set. This mirrors
350.   the analysis: contiguity is a kernel-stack requirement, explicitly *not* a user
351.   property — modeling user frames as ordered would over-specify.
352. - **Honest, symmetric error specs.** Every fallible path states the `Err` frame
353.   condition (`v' == v`, vec emptied) — the "no-leak / all-or-nothing" guarantee —
354.   and, for the watermark paths, the bidirectional gate (`Err ⇔ !user_alloc_ok`).
355.   Kernel paths fail only on genuine unavailability (`free_count == 0` / no
356.   contiguous run), stated as an interface predicate rather than a list of code
357.   checks.
358. 
359. ---
360. 
361. ## 7. Rejected alternatives
362. 
363. 1. **A new wrapper `PhysManagerView { frames: FrameAllocView }`.** Rejected. It
364.    carries exactly one field already named by `FrameAllocView`; the wrapper adds
365.    indirection and a second name for the same partition with no caller-visible
366.    information. `type V = FrameAllocView` is the minimal honest model. (Contrast
367.    phys-mod, where the wrapper *earned its keep* by adding two liveness bits.)
368. 
369. 2. **Mirror the implementation: fields `upool: UpoolView`, `init_flag: bool`.**
370.    Rejected. `upool` is internal bookkeeping over the *same* frames the partition
371.    already models; exposing it leaks the pool mechanism, fails the substitution
372.    test (a free-list rewrite has no `Upool`), and duplicates state. The init flag
373.    is structurally implied by holding `&mut self`.
374. 
375. 3. **Put the watermark (`free_count >= W`) into `inv()`.** Rejected as a false
376.    spec: kernel allocations deliberately drop free frames below `W`, so it is not
377.    an invariant. It belongs as the per-user-alloc gate `user_alloc_ok`.
378. 
379. 4. **Add a separate `free_count: nat` field to the View.** Rejected.
380.    `free_frames.len()` already determines it; a separate field would create a
381.    consistency obligation (`free_count == free_frames.len()`) for zero gain. Keep
382.    it derived.
383. 
384. 5. **Model returned user frames as an ordered `Seq` (like kernel frames).**
385.    Rejected. The analysis states user frames are mapped individually and their
386.    order is not caller-observable; a `Set` is the right abstraction and avoids
387.    over-specifying. Only kernel bulk needs order (contiguity).
388. 
389. 6. **Spec the manager over `phys_view()` (the free accessor) instead of
390.    `self@`.** Rejected for these functions. They are `&mut self`, so `self@` /
391.    `old(self)@` is the natural and Verus-native transition handle; routing
392.    through the global accessor would forfeit that and force a token argument into
393.    every contract. The relationship `self@ == phys_view().frames` is recorded as
394.    a proof-phase attachment invariant (§8), not pushed into the contracts.
395. 
396. 7. **Promise full state preservation on *every* error including a hypothetical
397.    mid-bulk failure.** Accepted here (`v' == v`) *because* the bulk paths are
398.    genuinely all-or-nothing (watermark checked up front; on any later per-frame
399.    failure the vec is cleared, freeing everything). This is sound — unlike
400.    phys-mod's booking, which is non-transactional and could only promise `inv()`.
401.

408. (whose only field, `upool`, is bookkeeping over those same frames). The proof
409. phase pins the closed mapping via the same ghost-token attachment `PhysModView`
410. uses, with the cross-View invariant:
411. 
412. - `self@`            ↔ `frame::INSTANCE@` (the verified `View for Inner`), and
413. - `self@ == phys_view().frames` whenever `phys_view().manager_ready`.

415. `free_count`, `user_alloc_ok`, `alloc_one`, and the contiguity helper are open
416. and computed purely from that `FrameAllocView`, so all six contracts in §4 are
417. the fixed target the token machinery must satisfy and do not change. (Same
418. pattern the bump-allocator and phys-mod Views used to defer their global-token
419. attachments.)

 # View Design: `mm::phys::manager` (`PhysMemoryManager`)
 
 > Phase output. Designs the abstract `View` that all later specs
 > (`requires`/`ensures`) for the six in-scope functions will reference:
 > `init`, `alloc_user_frame`, `check_user_watermark`,
 > `alloc_many_user_frames`, `alloc_many_kernel_frames`, `alloc_kernel_frame`.

 > `Inner::inv`, `frame_addr_of`, `View for Inner`, `Inner::internal_inv`) and
 > the already-committed subsystem View `PhysModView` / `phys_view()`.
 
 ---
 
 ## 1. Abstract Resource (from caller analysis)
 
 To its callers (`mm/virt`, all through `unsafe { get_mut() }`), the
 `PhysMemoryManager` is the **singleton broker over the global pool of physical
 page frames**. It hands out *typed, owning frame handles*:
 
 - **`KernelFrame`s** — drawn straight from the frame allocator, **contiguous on
   request**, **never watermark-gated** (kernel allocation must succeed whenever
   *any* physical frame is free).
 - **`UserFrame`s** — drawn for user mappings and **watermark-gated**: a user
   request is rejected (`OutOfMemory`) if fulfilling it would drop the number of
   free frames below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`, so the kernel always keeps a reserve.
 
 The only abstract state these six functions observe or mutate is therefore the
 **frame partition**: which physical frames are allocated vs. free, with
 per-frame refcounts, and — derived from it — *how many frames are free* (the
 quantity the watermark gate reads). That partition is **already** modeled by the
 do-not-modify `FrameAllocView` (== the verified `View for Inner` of the global
 `frame::INSTANCE`, and == `PhysModView.frames`).
 
 Callers explicitly **do not** observe: the `upool` internals, the
 `MaybeUninit`/`AtomicBool` singleton storage, the watermark *threshold value*,
 the chosen physical addresses, or how contiguity is obtained. They observe only:
 *which frames became reserved*, *that user paths enforce the watermark*, *that
 kernel bulk frames are contiguous*, and the *all-or-nothing / no-leak* error
 behavior.
 
 ---
 
 ## 2. The View — reuse `FrameAllocView`, add no new struct
 
 Because the six functions are `&mut self` methods, Verus already gives us the
 `old(self)@ -> self@` transition pair for free — no global-token deferral is
 needed for the *receiver* (unlike phys-mod's free functions). The receiver's
 abstract state is exactly the frame partition it brokers, which is precisely
 `FrameAllocView`. Wrapping it in a new one-field struct would add indirection
 and zero information, so:
 
 ```rust
 impl View for PhysMemoryManager {
     type V = FrameAllocView;
 
     // Closed: the manager brokers the *global* frame partition (frame::INSTANCE).
     // The concrete mapping to that singleton is pinned in the proof phase by the
     // same ghost-token attachment PhysModView uses (see §8); here it is read like
     // any `self@`.
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> FrameAllocView;
 }
 ```
 
 So `self@ : FrameAllocView`, and every spec for these functions speaks the
 **existing frame-partition vocabulary** (`reserved`, `all_free`, `covers`,
 `book_all`, the `allocated_frames`/`free_frames`/`refcounts` fields) plus the
 small allocation/watermark extensions in §2.1.
 
 ### 2.1 Derived spec helpers (new `impl FrameAllocView` block — existing `struct`/`wf` untouched)
 
 ```rust
 impl FrameAllocView {
     /// Number of frames currently free, i.e. available to hand out. This is the
     /// single quantity the kernel watermark reads. Models `frame::free_count()`.
     pub open spec fn free_count(self) -> nat {
         self.free_frames.len()
     }
 
     /// A user allocation of `count` frames is admissible: fulfilling it would
     /// still leave at least `KERNEL_WATERMARK` frames free for the kernel.
     /// This is the predicate behind the user-vs-kernel asymmetry — the gate
     /// `check_user_watermark` enforces. Reads the build-time constant directly
     /// so callers need not thread the threshold through.
     pub open spec fn user_alloc_ok(self, count: nat) -> bool {
         self.free_count() >= count + (config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK as nat)
     }
 
     /// Allocate a single currently-free frame `addr`: move it free -> allocated
     /// with refcount 1. (== `book_all(set![addr])`; spelled out for readability.)
     pub open spec fn alloc_one(self, addr: int) -> FrameAllocView {
         FrameAllocView {
             allocated_frames: self.allocated_frames.insert(addr),
             free_frames: self.free_frames.remove(addr),
             refcounts: self.refcounts.insert(addr, 1),
         }
     }
 }
 ```
 
 The set-at-once transition already exists as the do-not-modify
 `FrameAllocView::book_all(set)` — reused verbatim for the bulk paths.
 Contiguity reuses the do-not-modify `region_frame_addrs(base, size)` (the set of
 page-aligned frame addresses of `[base, base+size)`).
 
 ---
 
 ## 3. Well-formedness Invariant `inv()`
 
 ```rust
 impl PhysMemoryManager {
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         // The brokered frame partition is well formed: free/allocated disjoint,
         // page-aligned, refcount<->allocated consistent, refcounts in 1..=255.
         self@.wf()
     }
 }
 ```
 
 `inv()` is just `self@.wf()` and nothing more, on purpose:
 
 - **Liveness is structural.** Possessing `&mut self` (only obtainable from
   `get_mut()` after `init` succeeded) already witnesses `manager_ready`; there is
   no separate "is-up" bit for these methods to carry. The cross-layer liveness
   fact lives in `PhysModView` (`manager_ready ==> initialized`) and is the
   business of `phys::init`, not of the per-allocation contracts.
 - **The watermark is NOT an invariant.** "≥ `KERNEL_WATERMARK` frames free" holds
   only *after a user allocation*; kernel allocations are designed to dip below
   it. So it is a per-user-alloc **gate** (`user_alloc_ok`), never a type
   invariant. Putting it in `inv()` would be a false spec that kernel allocation
   legitimately violates.
 
 ---
 
 ## 4. Spec transitions of the target functions
 
 State is `v = old(self)@`, `v' = self@` (both `FrameAllocView`). `ps` =
 `spec_page_size()`, `W` = `KERNEL_WATERMARK`. Every clause is stated only over
 `FrameAllocView`; nothing names `upool`, the singleton storage, or the threshold
 value beyond `user_alloc_ok`.

 ensures   self.inv()
           match result {
             Ok(kf) => {
               // some previously-free frame is now reserved and owned by kf
               &&& v.free_frames.contains(kf.addr())
               &&& v' == v.alloc_one(kf.addr())
               // ⇒ v'.reserved(kf.addr())  and  v'.free_count() == v.free_count() - 1
             }
             Err(_) => {
               // nothing allocated, nothing leaked: partition unchanged
               &&& v' == v
               // failure ⇔ no frame was available at all (kernel never self-limits)
               &&& v.free_count() == 0

 `v.free_count() > 0 ==> result is Ok` is the contrapositive liveness fact a

 - **Reuse the frame partition; introduce no new struct.** The six functions'
   sole caller-observable effect is on the global frame partition, which
   `FrameAllocView` already abstracts (and which `frame`'s verified `View for
   Inner` and `PhysModView.frames` already use). Setting `type V = FrameAllocView`

   state and add indirection for no caller-visible gain.

   functions, these are methods, so `old(self)@ -> self@` *is* the v->v' pair; no
   per-call global-token ceremony is needed in the contracts (only the closed
   `view()` mapping is pinned in proof — §8).

   (`free_count >= count + W`) is the one predicate distinguishing user from
   kernel allocation. It appears as a precondition-equivalent in the user paths
   and is deliberately absent from `inv()` because kernel allocation is *meant*
   to breach it. `check_user_watermark`'s contract is exactly this predicate, so
   both user paths provably share one gate.

   `alloc_one(addr)` describe the entire effect declaratively; `all_reserved`,
   `free_count` decrements, and "booked ⇒ never re-handed-out" all follow, so each
   ensures is a clause the caller drops straight into a proof.

   `frames@[i].addr() == base + i*ps`; user bulk states only a set. This mirrors
   the analysis: contiguity is a kernel-stack requirement, explicitly *not* a user
   property — modeling user frames as ordered would over-specify.

   condition (`v' == v`, vec emptied) — the "no-leak / all-or-nothing" guarantee —
   and, for the watermark paths, the bidirectional gate (`Err ⇔ !user_alloc_ok`).

   contiguous run), stated as an interface predicate rather than a list of code
   checks.
 
 ---

 1. **A new wrapper `PhysManagerView { frames: FrameAllocView }`.** Rejected. It
    carries exactly one field already named by `FrameAllocView`; the wrapper adds
    indirection and a second name for the same partition with no caller-visible
    information. `type V = FrameAllocView` is the minimal honest model. (Contrast
    phys-mod, where the wrapper *earned its keep* by adding two liveness bits.)
 
 2. **Mirror the implementation: fields `upool: UpoolView`, `init_flag: bool`.**
    Rejected. `upool` is internal bookkeeping over the *same* frames the partition
    already models; exposing it leaks the pool mechanism, fails the substitution
    test (a free-list rewrite has no `Upool`), and duplicates state. The init flag
    is structurally implied by holding `&mut self`.

    spec: kernel allocations deliberately drop free frames below `W`, so it is not
    an invariant. It belongs as the per-user-alloc gate `user_alloc_ok`.

    `free_frames.len()` already determines it; a separate field would create a
    consistency obligation (`free_count == free_frames.len()`) for zero gain. Keep
    it derived.

    Rejected. The analysis states user frames are mapped individually and their
    order is not caller-observable; a `Set` is the right abstraction and avoids

 6. **Spec the manager over `phys_view()` (the free accessor) instead of
    `self@`.** Rejected for these functions. They are `&mut self`, so `self@` /

    through the global accessor would forfeit that and force a token argument into

    a proof-phase attachment invariant (§8), not pushed into the contracts.

    mid-bulk failure.** Accepted here (`v' == v`) *because* the bulk paths are
    genuinely all-or-nothing (watermark checked up front; on any later per-frame

    phys-mod's booking, which is non-transactional and could only promise `inv()`.

 pattern the bump-allocator and phys-mod Views used to defer their global-token

 - **No leak on failure**: every error path frees frames already taken from the
   allocator (kernel wrap-failure free, contiguous-range cleanup, user-pool
   `clear`).
 - **Ownership/Drop discipline**: returned `KernelFrame`/`UserFrame` own their
   physical frame; dropping frees it, `leak()` transfers ownership. Callers manage
   frame lifetime entirely through these handles.
 - **Caller-supplied storage contract**: bulk APIs require the passed `Vec` to be
   empty with `capacity ≥ count`; otherwise `InvalidArgument`.
 
 ## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
 - Source: added during verification of the enclosing `mm::phys` module
   (`mod.rs` / `mod.spec.rs`).
 - View type: exists — `PhysModView` with field `frames: FrameAllocView`, plus
   `initialized` and `manager_ready` flags; accessed via `phys_view()`. The
   manager-specific spec file `manager.spec.rs` is currently an empty `verus!{}`
   block (no per-function specs yet).
 - Functions WITH specs touching the manager: only `init` participates indirectly
   — `mm/phys/mod.rs::init` ensures `phys_view().live()` after calling
   `PhysMemoryManager::init` + `lemma_manager_ready()`. `PhysMemoryManager::init`
   itself is `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` (no requires/ensures of its own).
 - Functions WITHOUT specs: `alloc_kernel_frame`, `alloc_many_kernel_frames`,
   `alloc_many_user_frames`, `alloc_user_frame`, `check_user_watermark` — none
   carry `verus_spec` yet.
 
 ### Assessment
 - Coverage: partial. The upstream work modeled subsystem *liveness*
   (`initialized` / `manager_ready` / `frames.wf()`) and reservation vocabulary on
   `FrameAllocView`, which is what `phys::init` needed. It did **not** specify the
   allocation operations.
 - Strength: weak for this module's purpose. There is no spec expressing the
   watermark gate, the allocated/free refcount transitions per alloc, contiguity
   for kernel ranges, or the all-or-nothing/no-leak error behavior callers rely
   on. `PhysMemoryManager::init` being `external_body` with no ensures means the
   `manager_ready` transition is currently asserted only via `lemma_manager_ready`.
 - View design: the existing `FrameAllocView` (allocated/free sets + refcounts) is
   caller-abstract and is the right basis for the alloc specs — it already exposes
   exactly what callers observe (which frames are taken, refcounts for CoW).
   Remaining work is to write per-function ensures over `phys_view().frames` for
   the six target functions; do **not** modify `FrameAllocView`, `Inner`,
   `frame_addr_of`, `byte_at_address`, or the `View for Inner` impl.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. // PhysMemoryManager - Specifications
5. //
6. // This file contains specification functions and view types.
7. 
8. verus! {
9. 
10. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
11. use vstd::map::*;
12. 
13. pub uninterp spec fn byte_at_address(ptr: int) -> u8;
14. 
15. /// Abstract view of the frame allocator (`frame::Inner`).
16. ///
17. /// Captures which physical frames are currently allocated vs. free,
18. /// together with a per-frame reference count that models shared
19. /// ownership (e.g. copy-on-write after `share()`).
20. pub struct FrameAllocView
21. {
22.     pub allocated_frames: Set<int>,
23.     pub free_frames: Set<int>,
24.     /// Maps each allocated frame address to its reference count.
25.     /// A frame is present in the map iff it is currently allocated.
26.     pub refcounts: Map<int, int>,
27. }
28. 
29. impl FrameAllocView
30. {
31.     pub open spec fn wf(&self) -> bool
32.     {
33.         // Page-alignment
34.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
35.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
36.         // Disjoint
37.         &&& self.allocated_frames.disjoint(self.free_frames)
38.         // Allocated ↔ refcount consistency: a frame is allocated iff it has a positive refcount
39.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) <==>
40.             self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) && self.refcounts[addr] > 0
41.         // Free frames have no refcount entry
42.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==>
43.             !self.refcounts.contains_key(addr)
44.         // Refcount bounded by u8 range
45.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) ==>
46.             0 < self.refcounts[addr] <= 255
47.     }
48. }
49. 
50. //==================================================================================================
51. // LinkedList — external type registration
52. //==================================================================================================
53. //
54. // `vstd` provides no specification for `alloc::collections::LinkedList`, so it must be
55. // registered as an external type before it can appear in spec signatures. Only the type
56. // is registered here; no `View`/iterator specification is provided, because the orphan
57. // rule forbids a downstream crate from implementing vstd's `View` / `ForLoopGhostIterator`
58. // traits for the foreign `LinkedList` / `linked_list::Iter` types. As a consequence, the
59. // two helpers that iterate a `LinkedList` in a `for` loop (`book_physical_memory_regions`,
60. // `book_mmio_regions`) cannot have their bodies verified and are `external_body`. See
61. // `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-mod/bugs.md`.
62. 
63. use ::core::alloc::Allocator;
64. 
65. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
66. #[verifier::external_body]
67. #[verifier::accept_recursive_types(T)]
68. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
69. pub struct ExLinkedList<T, A: Allocator>(::alloc::collections::LinkedList<T, A>);
70. 
71. //==================================================================================================
72. // Physical-memory subsystem view
73. //==================================================================================================
74. 
75. /// Abstract view of the global physical-memory subsystem managed by `mm::phys`.
76. ///
77. /// Pure ghost description — names no `MaybeUninit`, `AtomicBool`, bitmap, refcount slice,
78. /// or any other storage mechanism. It wraps the existing frame-allocator view
79. /// (`FrameAllocView`) with the two liveness facts the caller depends on.
80. pub ghost struct PhysModView {
81.     /// The frame allocator singleton has been initialized (`frame::init` ran
82.     /// successfully). All `frames`-related guarantees are meaningful only when this holds.
83.     pub initialized: bool,
84.     /// Abstract frame-allocator state: which physical frames are allocated (reserved) vs.
85.     /// free, with per-frame refcounts. This is the existing `FrameAllocView`.
86.     pub frames: FrameAllocView,
87.     /// The `PhysMemoryManager` singleton has been initialized with a fresh user page pool.
88.     pub manager_ready: bool,
89. }
90. 
91. /// Current abstract state of the global physical-memory subsystem.
92. ///
93. /// Uninterpreted accessor: the subsystem state lives in module-level singletons
94. /// (`frame::INSTANCE`/`INSTANCE_INIT` and the `PhysMemoryManager`/`Upool` singletons)
95. /// whose value is not directly spec-readable. The cross-call transition (`v -> v'`) is
96. /// realized in the proving phase by a ghost token over those singletons (see
97. /// `view_design.md` section 8); during the specification phase it is read like `self@`.
98. pub uninterp spec fn phys_view() -> PhysModView;
99. 
100. impl PhysModView {
101.     /// Well-formedness invariant of the subsystem.
102.     pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
103.         // Once the allocator is up, the frame partition is well formed.
104.         &&& self.initialized ==> self.frames.wf()
105.         // The manager layer can only be up if the allocator is up.
106.         &&& self.manager_ready ==> self.initialized
107.     }
108. 
109.     /// The subsystem is fully brought up and self-consistent.
110.     pub open spec fn live(self) -> bool {
111.         &&& self.initialized
112.         &&& self.manager_ready
113.         &&& self.frames.wf()
114.     }
115. }
116. 
117. //==================================================================================================
118. // Frame-set vocabulary (on the existing FrameAllocView)
119. //==================================================================================================
120. 
121. impl FrameAllocView {
122.     /// The allocator tracks (covers) the frame at `addr` — it is one of the frames this
123.     /// allocator knows about, allocated or free. Models `frame::is_covered`.
124.     pub open spec fn covers(self, addr: int) -> bool {
125.         self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) || self.free_frames.contains(addr)
126.     }
127. 
128.     /// The frame at `addr` is reserved: present in the allocated set, hence `alloc()` can
129.     /// never return it. This is the core caller-visible fact a "booked" frame satisfies.
130.     pub open spec fn reserved(self, addr: int) -> bool {
131.         self.allocated_frames.contains(addr)
132.     }
133. 
134.     /// Every frame address in `set` is reserved.
135.     pub open spec fn all_reserved(self, set: Set<int>) -> bool {
136.         forall|a: int| set.contains(a) ==> self.reserved(a)
137.     }
138. 
139.     /// Every frame address in `set` is currently free (booking precondition: a range can be
140.     /// booked only if it is entirely free).
141.     pub open spec fn all_free(self, set: Set<int>) -> bool {
142.         forall|a: int| #[trigger] set.contains(a) ==> self.free_frames.contains(a)
143.     }
144. 
145.     /// Reserve every frame in `set` (each assumed free in `self`): move it from
146.     /// `free_frames` to `allocated_frames` with refcount 1.
147.     pub open spec fn book_all(self, set: Set<int>) -> FrameAllocView {
148.         FrameAllocView {
149.             allocated_frames: self.allocated_frames.union(set),
150.             free_frames: self.free_frames.difference(set),
151.             refcounts: self.refcounts.union_prefer_right(
152.                 Map::new(|a: int| set.contains(a), |a: int| 1int),
153.             ),
154.         }
155.     }
156. 
157.     /// Reserve only the *covered* frames of `set`; skip the rest (coverage-gated). Models
158.     /// the MMIO booking rule.
159.     pub open spec fn book_covered(self, set: Set<int>) -> FrameAllocView {
160.         self.book_all(set.filter(|a: int| self.covers(a)))
161.     }
162. }
163. 
164. /// Page-aligned physical frame addresses covered by a region `[start, start + size)`.
165. /// Mirrors the frame-set computation used by `frame::alloc_range`.
166. pub open spec fn region_frame_addrs(start: int, size: int) -> Set<int> {
167.     let start_frame_number = start / spec_page_size();
168.     let end_frame_number = (start + size) / spec_page_size();
169.     vstd::set_lib::set_int_range(start_frame_number, end_frame_number)
170.         .map(|i: int| i * spec_page_size())
171. }
172. 
173. /// The set of physical frame addresses covered by all regions in a physical
174. /// non-usable-memory list. Uninterpreted: `LinkedList` has no Verus model, so its contents
175. /// cannot be folded over in spec; this names the abstract union of `region_frame_addrs`
176. /// over the list, which is all the contract needs.
177. pub uninterp spec fn phys_regions_frame_set(
178.     regions: &::alloc::collections::LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>>,
179. ) -> Set<int>;
180. 
181. /// The set of physical frame addresses covered by all MMIO regions in a list (after
182. /// GVA->GPA translation). Uninterpreted for the same reason as `phys_regions_frame_set`.
183. pub uninterp spec fn mmio_regions_frame_set(
184.     regions: &::alloc::collections::LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<VirtualAddress>>,
185. ) -> Set<int>;
186. 
187. } // end verus!
188.

620. // Use relaxed ordering for all atomic operations to mitigate synchronization overhead. It is safe
621. // to use this ordering semantics because Nanvix is a single-core system, and the kernel runs with
622. // interrupts disabled.
623. const ORDER: Ordering = Ordering::Relaxed;
624. 
625. //==================================================================================================
626. // Singleton
627. //==================================================================================================
628. 
629. /// Module-level singleton storage.
630. static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner> = MaybeUninit::uninit();
631. 
632. /// Whether the frame allocator has been initialized.
633. static INSTANCE_INIT: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);
634. 
635. /// Returns a mutable reference to the initialized singleton.
636. fn instance() -> &'static mut Inner {
637.     if unlikely(!INSTANCE_INIT.load(ORDER)) {
638.         panic!("frame allocator used before init()");
639.     }
640. 
641.     // SAFETY: `INSTANCE_INIT` is `true`, so `INSTANCE` has been fully written by `init()`.
642.     // The kernel is single-threaded with interrupts disabled, so no concurrent access is possible.
643.     unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }
644. }
645. 
646. //==================================================================================================
647. // Public Free Functions
648. //==================================================================================================
649. 
650. /// Initialize the frame allocator singleton.
651. ///
652. /// # Safety
653. ///
654. /// Must be called exactly once during boot, before any other function
655. /// in this module.
656. #[verus_verify(external_body)]
657. pub(super) unsafe fn init(bitmap: Bitmap) -> Result<(), Error> {
658.     if unlikely(INSTANCE_INIT.load(ORDER)) {
659.         return Err(Error::new(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, "frame allocator already initialized"));
660.     }
661. 
662.     info!(
663.         "frame allocator: {} frames, {} MB",
664.         bitmap.number_of_bits(),
665.         (bitmap.number_of_bits() * mem::FRAME_SIZE) / constants::MEGABYTE,
666.     );
667. 
668.     let nframes: usize = bitmap.number_of_bits();
669.     if nframes > NFRAMES {
670.         return Err(Error::new(
671.             ErrorCode::InvalidArgument,
672.             "frame bitmap is larger than the configured refcount storage",
673.         ));
674.     }
675. 
676.     // SAFETY: single-threaded boot; no other reference to `REFCOUNT_STORAGE` exists.
677.     let refcount: &'static mut [u8] = unsafe { &mut REFCOUNT_STORAGE[..] };
678. 
679.     // Defensively sync refcounts with any bits already set in the incoming bitmap. The
680.     // current microvm boot path supplies an empty bitmap and performs all reservations
681.     // via `book()` / `alloc_range()` after `init()`, so this loop normally does nothing.
682.     // It is kept as a safety net so a future boot path that hands us a pre-populated
683.     // bitmap (for example to express firmware-reserved regions) does not silently end
684.     // up with `bitmap bit = 1, refcount = 0`, which would cause the first `free()` of
685.     // such a frame to be rejected as a spurious double-free.
686.     for (i, slot) in refcount.iter_mut().enumerate().take(nframes) {
687.         if matches!(bitmap.test(i), Ok(true)) {
688.             *slot = 1;
689.         }
690.     }
691. 
692.     // SAFETY: single-threaded boot; no other reference to `INSTANCE` exists.
693.     unsafe { INSTANCE.write(Inner { bitmap, refcount }) };
694.     INSTANCE_INIT.store(true, ORDER);
695.     Ok(())
696. }
697. 
698. /// Allocate a frame.
699. pub(super) fn alloc() -> Result<FrameAddress, Error> {
700.     instance().alloc()
701. }
702. 
703. /// # Description
704. ///
705. /// Allocates `count` physically contiguous frames.
706. ///
707. /// # Returns
708. ///
709. /// Returns the base `FrameAddress` of the contiguous range.
710. ///
711. pub(super) fn alloc_contiguous(count: usize) -> Result<FrameAddress, Error> {
712.     instance().alloc_contiguous(count)
713. }
714. 
715. ///
716. /// # Description
717. ///
718. /// Returns the number of free frames in the system.
719. ///
720. /// # Returns
721. ///
722. /// The number of free frames in the system.
723. ///
724. pub(super) fn free_count() -> usize {
725.     let inner = instance();
726.     inner.bitmap.number_of_bits() - inner.bitmap.usage()
727. }
728. 
729. /// Free a frame previously returned by [`alloc`].
730. pub(super) fn free(frame: FrameAddress) -> Result<(), Error> {
731.     instance().free(frame)
732. }
733. 
734. ///

name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.
   3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
   5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
      assumption was checked against.

   - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.
   
   `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
   must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
   what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
   (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
   (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:

   Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
   ```
   self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
   self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
   self@.field_c == new_value,
   // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
   ```
   Good (complete by construction):
   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```
   This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
   inline or via spec transition functions.
7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
   `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
   single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
   prevents accidentally omitting one arm:

   Bad:
   ```
   ensures
       result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
   ```

   ensures match result {

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.

      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"

     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function

### Error Path Spec Principles

Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
with the same rigor as the success path.

1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.
2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract
   predicates on the module's interface state, not as a list of individual
   code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
   impossible?
3. **Liveness** — if the preconditions and current state make success
   possible, the spec must guarantee success (i.e., the function must
   not spuriously return `None`/`Err`). A spec that *allows* failure
   even when success is achievable is under-specified — callers cannot
   rely on it. Use `match` on the return value to specify both arms:
   ```
   ensures match result {
       Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
       Err(e) => /* error postcondition */,
   }
   ```
   This makes both arms visible for review — neither path is silently omitted.

### Where NOT to Invest Spec Effort

**Completely skip** (no spec needed at all):
- **Type-system guarantees** — ownership, borrow rules, type matching
- **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
- **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations

**Basic ensures only** (no additional spec design):
- **Trivial accessors** — field getters still need
  `ensures result == self@.field` for callers to reason about, but
  warrant no further properties.
- **Pure wrappers** — functions that directly delegate to a single
  verified function with no additional logic.

### Property Coverage Checklist

When writing specs, systematically cover these four dimensions for each
function and type. This ensures no important properties are missed.

1. **Functional Correctness** — What does the code achieve?
   - Preconditions (requires): what must the caller guarantee?
   - Success postconditions (ensures, Ok case): new abstract state, return value, frame condition
   - Error postconditions (ensures, Err case): state preservation, failure condition in abstract terms

2. **Safety** — What must never happen?
   - Bounds, disjointness, uniqueness, conservation, injectivity, ordering, monotonicity

3. **Liveness** — What good things must happen?
   - Guaranteed success conditions, resource availability, recoverability

4. **Structural Consistency** — Is the data self-consistent?
   - Type invariants, field relationships, valid ranges

### Invariant Design

Two kinds of invariants appear during specification:

- **Type invariant (`inv()`)** — defined on the View type (see **view-design**
  skill). Every constructor must establish it; every method must preserve it.
  If a property appears in `requires` of nearly every method, it belongs in
  `inv()` instead.
- **Loop invariant** — defined on loops. Must hold on entry (base case),
  be preserved by each iteration (inductive step), and together with the
  exit condition imply the function's `ensures` (sufficiency). Define
  complex invariants as `spec fn` predicates rather than inline clauses.

Both should reference View fields and abstract state, not implementation
details.

### Static vs Dynamic Condition Enforcement

**Key question**: Can this runtime check be statically eliminated through
verification?

**Yes → add `requires`**. The condition is provable from caller context
(e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.

**No → keep runtime check + Err**. The condition depends on inherently
dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
`requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.

**Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
`// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
verification work knows to clean it up.

### Post-Generation Spec Refinement

After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
   that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
   it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
   clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their
   proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
   form the caller actually needs.

## Part 2: Spec Classification

Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:

### Internal

Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.
**The AI generates these freely during proving.** The test for
correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
provides direct feedback.

### External-top (API contracts)

Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.

### External-bottom (trust assumptions)

Assumptions about layers below the verification scope: std library
behavior, hardware semantics, runtime correctness, compiler fidelity.
These are unverified: if they do not match reality, downstream proofs
may be unsound. Mechanisms include `assume_specification`,
`external_body`, and `axiom`. Which functions belong in this category
is pre-determined by the TCB allowed list — do not make new trust
boundary decisions during specification or proving.

### Rules

- The caller analysis and View design identify external-top properties.
- Trust boundary decisions (which functions get `external_body`) are
  pre-approved in the TCB allowed list. Do not classify new functions
  as trust boundaries — if a function is not in the list, it must be
  fully verified.
- When writing `assume_specification`, follow the audit checklist in
  Part 1 (Anti-Patterns, Verification Escape).

## Part 3: View Abstraction Design

The View type and a skeletal `inv()` should already be designed before writing
specifications. Refine and extend `inv()` as you write specs — new constraints
often emerge from requires/ensures. This section summarizes the key principles
for reference.

See `docs/specifying-and-proving-types.md` for the complete step-by-step guide
on View design, invariants, and method specifications.

1. **Only caller-visible state** — hide internal bookkeeping. Test: if you
   swapped the underlying data structure, would the View fields still make sense?
2. **Use abstract types** — `int` instead of `i32`, `Seq<int>` instead of
   `Vec<u64>`, `Map<K, V>` instead of `HashMap<K, V>`.
3. **`view()` is `pub closed spec fn`** — public so callers can invoke it,
   closed so implementation details don't leak.
4. **`inv()` is `pub open spec fn`** — includes `internal_inv()` plus
   abstraction-level properties (e.g., `self@.len() < usize::MAX`).
5. **No extra pub spec fns on `impl MyType`** beyond `inv` and `view`.
   Put reusable spec helpers on the View type instead.

For full View design methodology, see the **view-design** skill.

### Spec Transition Functions

For each state-mutating exec function, define a corresponding spec function
on the View type. Use `..self` to implicitly preserve unchanged fields
(frame condition):

```rust
impl FooView {
    pub open spec fn spec_insert(self, elem: int) -> FooView {
        FooView { elements: self.elements.insert(elem), ..self }
    }
}
// ensures self@ == old(self)@.spec_insert(elem as int)
```

**Do NOT** also list individual field changes as separate ensures — the
spec transition already captures the complete state change.

When modifying a collection element without a spec transition, state the
frame explicitly:
